oneSentence: Digitally produced or heavily altered images, audio, video or text can resemble real recordings or documents, even when no such original event or speaker existed.
plainExplanation:
Synthetic media means media files made or substantially changed by software, often using machine learning. The input can be a text prompt, a source image, a voice sample, a video clip, or a mix of these. The output can be new text, pictures, speech, music or video.

A common pattern is simple: a person gives instructions or example material, the system finds patterns from training data, and it generates a new result that matches those patterns. “Training data” means the examples used to tune the system before you use it. The result may look realistic, but realistic does not mean authentic.

This term is broader than “deepfake”. A deepfake usually means a synthetic or manipulated audio or video piece made to imitate a real person closely. Synthetic media also includes harmless or useful things, such as translated voice-overs, draft illustrations, accessibility narration or simulated training videos.

People often confuse synthetic media with synthetic data. They are related but different. Synthetic media is made for people to watch, hear or read. Synthetic data is usually made for analysis, testing or model training, not mainly for human audiences.

The key question is not only “Was AI used?” but also “What is this supposed to represent?” A generated image may be fine as an illustration if labelled clearly. The same image becomes a problem if it is presented as evidence of a real event.

everydayAnalogy.title: A poster team building a scene from parts
everydayAnalogy.story: A communications team needs a poster about safe water storage for a public campaign. They do not have a photo of the exact scene they want, so they describe it, choose colours, and combine elements that resemble many real photos they have seen before. The software produces an image of a family, containers and a background that looks convincing. Viewers may assume the moment really happened, even though it was assembled digitally for illustration.

mapping.analogyElement: The written description for the poster
mapping.aiElement: A text prompt or other input given to a generative system

mapping.analogyElement: The software combining familiar visual patterns
mapping.aiElement: A model generating media from patterns learned during training

mapping.analogyElement: Viewers assuming the scene was photographed
mapping.aiElement: Authenticity risk when generated content looks like evidence

everydayAnalogy.limitation: A design team usually works slowly and deliberately, while many synthetic media tools can produce many variations in seconds. Also, in the analogy, people manually choose parts they can inspect. Real generative systems do not literally paste together visible pieces from a small set of photos; they calculate outputs from learned statistical patterns, so the process is less transparent.

visual.title: How synthetic media is made and why context matters
visual.learningObjective: After viewing this, a reader should be able to explain that synthetic media starts from prompts or source files, is generated by a model, and then must be judged for purpose and authenticity.
visual.description: A left-to-right flow diagram with four boxes: Inputs, Generation, Output, and Use Context. Arrows connect each box. Below the final two boxes, a green tag reads “clearly labelled illustration” and a red tag reads “falsely presented as real evidence”. Read from left to right, then compare the two outcome tags.

steps.label: Inputs
steps.explanation: A person provides a prompt, source image, voice sample, video clip, or other instructions.
steps.visualInstruction: Draw a rounded rectangle labelled 'Inputs' with small icons for text, image, microphone and video inside.

steps.label: Generation
steps.explanation: A trained model uses learned patterns to produce a new media file or alter an existing one.
steps.visualInstruction: Draw a second rounded rectangle labelled 'Generation model'. Show gears or layered nodes, but keep them simple and abstract.

steps.label: Output
steps.explanation: The result may be text, image, speech, music or video that appears polished or realistic.
steps.visualInstruction: Draw a third rounded rectangle labelled 'Output' with thumbnail icons for document, picture, waveform and play button.

steps.label: Use context
steps.explanation: The same output can be acceptable as labelled illustration or misleading if presented as a record of reality.
steps.visualInstruction: Draw a fourth rounded rectangle labelled 'Use context' splitting into two tags below: green 'Labelled synthetic example' and red 'Claimed as real evidence'.

visual.interaction: Hover or tap each box to reveal one short example: prompt, model action, output type, and context label.
visual.accessibilityDescription: The diagram is a four-step flow from left to right. First, a user supplies inputs such as text instructions, an image, a voice sample or a video clip. Second, a generation model creates or alters media using patterns learned during training. Third, the system outputs text, images, audio or video that may look or sound realistic. Fourth, the meaning depends on use context: if the output is clearly labelled as synthetic or illustrative, it may be appropriate; if it is presented as proof of a real event or real speaker, it can mislead.
visual.reducedMotionDescription: Show the same four boxes and arrows without animation. Keep both end labels visible at all times: green for clearly labelled synthetic content, red for content falsely presented as real.

workedExample.scenario: A local health office wants a short awareness clip in three languages but has no filming budget for each version.
workedExample.input: Text script: 'Wash hands with soap for 20 seconds before preparing food.' Source: approved original script and a licensed presenter image for illustration only.
process: Staff use a tool to generate three voice-overs from the approved script in Arabic, French and Swahili.
They create a simple animated video with synthetic narration and on-screen text.
They add a clear note in the closing frame: 'Illustrative AI-generated voice and visuals; health guidance approved by the office.'
A reviewer checks that no real person is being impersonated and that the translation matches the approved message.
workedExample.result: The office publishes an accessible awareness clip that is useful for outreach because it is clearly labelled and not presented as a recording of a real event.

unWorkplaceExample.scenario: A team preparing a public situation report wants a short explainer video showing possible logistics bottlenecks after flooding.
unWorkplaceExample.relevance: Synthetic media can help create clearly labelled illustrative maps, narration and animations quickly when no suitable footage exists, making complex information easier to explain to non-specialists.
unWorkplaceExample.caution: Do not upload confidential drafts, personal data, security-sensitive locations, survivor information, witness details or unapproved operational material into a public AI service. Do not present generated visuals as verified field evidence.

whyItMatters: Synthetic media affects trust. It can save time in communication, translation, accessibility and training, but it can also blur the line between illustration and evidence. Non-specialists need to ask basic questions: What was generated, what was edited, who made it, how is it labelled, and should it be treated as proof? Those questions help with safer communication, procurement, risk assessment and public trust.
whereYouMayHearIt: news about fake videos or cloned voices

commonMisconceptions.correction: Not always. Many uses are legitimate, such as clearly labelled illustrations, dubbing, accessibility narration or training materials. The risk comes from misleading context, weak disclosure or impersonation, not from every generated file.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: If it looks real, it must show a real event.
commonMisconceptions.correction: Realistic appearance is not proof of authenticity. A system can generate convincing faces, voices or scenes that never existed. Verification still needs source checks, metadata, corroboration or trusted provenance methods.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Synthetic media only means fake videos of politicians.
commonMisconceptions.correction: That is a narrow case. The term also covers generated images, speech, music, text and other media, including benign uses. Deepfakes are one subset, not the whole category.

simpleVsTechnical.simple: Synthetic media is media made or changed by software so that it may look, sound or read like something real, even when it was generated.
simpleVsTechnical.technical: Synthetic media refers to digitally generated or materially transformed media outputs, including text, images, audio and video, produced by computational systems such as generative models. Inputs may include prompts, conditioning signals, reference media or editing instructions. Depending on the system, generation may involve methods such as diffusion, adversarial training or other learned probabilistic mappings from input conditions to output content. The main issue is not only generation itself but provenance, disclosure and evidential status: whether the output is labelled, traceable and appropriate for its claimed use.

keyTakeaway: Synthetic media can be useful, but realistic content should not be treated as proof unless its source and context are verified.

quickCheck.question: Which statement best describes synthetic media?
options: Only fake videos made to deceive voters
Any media created or significantly altered by software, often using AI, including useful labelled content and misleading content
Only images produced from text prompts
Any digital file that has been compressed or edited
quickCheck.explanation: Synthetic media is a broad category. It includes generated or heavily altered text, images, audio and video. Some uses are benign and clearly labelled; others are deceptive. It is broader than deepfakes and narrower than all digital editing.
